unit.title: Comply with infection prevention and control policies and procedures

summary: This unit teaches you to follow the salon's infection prevention and control (IPC) policy so that germs are not passed from client to client, from client to therapist, or from therapist to client. You will learn how infection spreads, standard precautions, hand hygiene and PPE, the difference between cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation, how to treat tools, equipment, towels and the treatment area, how to deal with sharps, blood spills and waste, and how to keep records and report problems.

blocks.p: Every beauty treatment brings people, skin, tools and products together. Done carelessly, a manicure can spread a fungus, a wax can spread a skin infection and a blade can spread a blood-borne virus. **Infection prevention and control (IPC)** is the set of habits and procedures that stop germs spreading. The salon's **policy** says what must be done; the **procedures** say how.

This unit is for GENERAL BEAUTY THERAPY LEVEL 2 trainees and applies to every treatment you will give: nails, waxing, facials, massage, lashes and more. It is about **complying**: doing the correct steps every time, even when the salon is busy and nobody is watching. A client who gets an infection from a salon may be seriously ill, may take the salon to court and will tell everyone she knows.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: a theory paper (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's salon: cleaning, disinfecting and resetting a manicure and pedicure station between clients, then dealing with a mock blood spill, setting up a sharps box and sorting mock waste. No real blood is used. The assessor watches your order of work, your PPE, your timing and your teamwork.

sections.title: How infection spreads and what the policy requires

blocks.p: A **pathogen** is a germ that can cause disease: a bacterium, a virus, a fungus or a parasite. **Micro-organisms** is the scientific word for living things too small to see without a microscope. Most are harmless. Some live on healthy skin; others live in water, soil and dirt.

head: Germ
Salon examples
rows: Bacteria
Impetigo, boils, infected cuts, folliculitis (infected hair follicles after waxing or shaving)
Viruses
Warts and verrucas, cold sores, hepatitis B and C, HIV, colds and flu
Fungi
Athlete's foot, ringworm, fungal nail infection
Parasites
Head lice, scabies

blocks.p: Some bacteria can form tough **spores** that survive normal disinfection. Only sterilisation can be relied on to kill spores.

flow: A pathogen is present
It lives and multiplies in a reservoir (a person, tool, water, dirt)
It leaves through a portal of exit (a wound, blood, cough)
It is carried by a route (hands, tools, towels, air)
It enters through a portal of entry (cut, graze, eyes, nose, mouth)
It reaches a susceptible person (one who can catch it)

blocks.p: Good practice aims to **break the chain at one or more links**. For example: clean tools remove the reservoir, gloves block the route, a waterproof plaster closes a portal of entry, a vaccine protects the susceptible person.

head: Way in (portal of entry)
Example
rows: Broken skin
A cut, graze, crack in the skin of the heels, a hangnail, a recently waxed or exfoliated area
Eyes, nose and mouth
Touching your face with dirty hands; splashes
Breathing in
Droplets, dust
Swallowing
Eating or drinking with unwashed hands

blocks.h: Routes of spread in a salon

head: Route
Example in the salon
rows: Direct contact
Skin touching skin: a therapist's hands on a client with an infected rash
Indirect contact
A comb, file or towel used on one client and then on the next; a foot bowl that was not disinfected; a door handle
Blood and body fluids
A blade, nippers or tweezers that have drawn blood; a towel with blood on it
Droplets and airborne spread
A coughing client or therapist
Contaminated water and food
A dirty foot spa; unsafe drinking water; food kept in the treatment room

ul: Clients with a weak immune system: older people, babies, pregnant women, people with diabetes or HIV, or those on some medicines.
Clients with cuts, sores, eczema or recently treated skin.
You: when you have cuts, are tired, or are not vaccinated.

blocks.p: **Standard precautions** are the safe steps used with **every client, every time**, whether or not she looks or says she is well. You cannot tell by looking who has hepatitis B or HIV. They include hand hygiene, PPE, covering cuts, safe handling of sharps, cleaning and disinfecting of tools and surfaces, safe handling of waste and laundry, and quick clean-up of spills.

ul: The salon or Centre has a **written IPC policy and procedures**. It is based on guidance from the **Ministry of Health and Wellness** and on the instructions of the makers of products and equipment. Know where it is kept and read it.
**Everyone** follows it: managers, therapists, trainees, cleaners and visitors who work with clients. It is not only for the people who use sharp tools or wax.
Do not follow a friend's advice, a video or a client's suggestion in place of the policy. If you think the policy is wrong, tell your supervisor.
Report a breach, a near miss or a faulty piece of equipment. Reporting is not telling tales: it protects people.
Staff must be trained, and the training is recorded.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, health departments and the Ministry of Health and Wellness inspect premises where personal services are provided, and guidance can change. Ask your instructor for the policy the Centre follows.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Wear a **clean uniform** every day; change it if it is soiled or splashed.
Tie back long hair; keep your nails short, clean and free of polish chips or gel that could harbour germs.
Take off rings, bracelets and watches before treatments.
Cover every cut or sore on your hands with a waterproof plaster and gloves.
Do not work with an infection: a weeping rash on your hands, a fever, vomiting or diarrhoea. Report it and follow the sickness policy.
Do not eat, drink or smoke in the treatment area; do not touch your face, hair or phone during a treatment.

blocks.p: Clean your hands **before and after every client**, before putting on gloves and after taking them off, after touching soiled items or waste, after the toilet and before eating.

head: Method
When
Notes
rows: Soap and running water
When hands are visibly dirty or soiled, after the toilet, before eating, after blood or body fluids
Wet, soap, rub all surfaces (palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips, wrists) for at least **20 seconds**
Rinse, dry with a **clean single-use paper towel**, and use the towel to turn off the tap
Alcohol hand rub
When hands are not visibly dirty, between clients
At least **60% alcohol**
Rub all surfaces until dry, about 20 seconds
Does not clean dirt: wash if hands are dirty

head: PPE
Purpose
When to use it
rows: Disposable gloves
Protect your hands and the client from blood, body fluids, chemicals and broken skin
Waxing, extractions, cleaning tools, handling waste, soiled laundry and spills
Disposable apron
Protects your uniform from splashes and germs
Cleaning, mixing disinfectant, blood spills
Eye protection
Protects your eyes
Mixing or pouring chemicals, spills, tasks that could splash
Mask
Protects against droplets and dust
As the policy says: nail dust, powders, outbreaks

ul: **Change gloves between every client**, between dirty and clean tasks, and whenever they tear. Never wash or reuse disposable gloves.
Gloves are not a substitute for hand cleaning: clean your hands before putting on and after taking off.
Choose gloves for the task. Use latex-free gloves if you or a client is allergic to latex. Use chemical-resistant gloves, such as nitrile, for disinfectants.
Do not touch your face, hair, phone or door handles with gloves that you have used on a client.

flow: Clean your hands
Put on the apron
Put on the mask, if needed
Put on eye protection, if needed
Put on gloves, over the cuffs
After the task, remove gloves first, without touching the outside with bare hands
Remove eye protection and mask by the straps; remove the apron by rolling it inwards
Put items in the correct bin
Clean your hands again

blocks.p: These three words mean different things. Learn the differences, because the right level must be used for each item.

head: Level
What it does
How
Example
rows: **Cleaning**
Removes dirt, hair, skin, oil and product. Reduces germs but does not kill them all.
Detergent, warm water and a brush
Scrubbing used tweezers in warm soapy water
**Disinfection**
Kills most germs (not all spores) on clean tools and surfaces.
A chemical disinfectant, made up as the maker says, for the full contact time; or wiping surfaces
Soaking clean metal tools in disinfectant; wiping the couch and trolley
**Sterilisation**
Kills **all** germs, including spores.
An autoclave (steam under pressure), or heat or other methods approved by the maker and the policy
Sterilising reusable metal tools that may break the skin

blocks.note: Always **clean before you disinfect or sterilise**. Dirt, hair, skin and product shield germs, and they use up the disinfectant. A dirty tool put into disinfectant stays dirty.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Put on gloves and eye protection (and an apron)
Take used tools to a separate 'dirty' area; open hinged tools
Scrub with a brush in warm, soapy water, under the surface if possible, to avoid splashes
Rinse under clean running water
Check that no hair, skin or product is left; scrub again if there is
Dry the tool
Read the label and the safety data sheet
Measure the disinfectant and the water exactly as the maker says, in a labelled container with a lid
Put in the clean, dry tools so that every part is covered and no air is trapped
Time the full **contact time** from when the last tool goes in
Remove with clean tongs or gloves; rinse if the label says to
Dry with a clean single-use towel or in clean air
Store in a clean, closed, labelled container; replace the solution as the label says or when dirty

head: Point
What to know
rows: Contact time
How long the item must stay wet with disinfectant. It is on the label: it may be a few minutes or longer. Too short and the germs survive.
Dilution
Follow the maker. Too weak does not kill germs; too strong can damage skin, tools and surfaces, and give off fumes.
Fresh solution
Disinfectant weakens over time and when it gets dirty. Make it fresh as often as the label says, usually at least daily, and always when cloudy or dirty.
Type
Choose a disinfectant that is made for the item and approved by the policy. Alcohol-based, chlorine-based and other types have different uses.
Metals
Some disinfectants rust or damage metal if tools are left in too long. Follow the maker.
Surfaces
Wipe with detergent first, then apply disinfectant for its contact time and let it air-dry.

ul: An **autoclave** uses steam under pressure to kill all germs, including spores. Typical settings are about 121 °C for about 15 to 20 minutes, or about 134 °C for several minutes, but **follow the maker and the policy**.
Tools must be clean and dry first, and often are sealed in pouches that show a colour change when the cycle is done.
Keep the autoclave maintained, record each cycle and test it as the policy says.
Open it only when the cycle is finished, and store sterilised tools in their sealed pouches until needed.

blocks.note: A UV cabinet only **stores** tools that are already clean and disinfected. It does **not** clean, disinfect or sterilise dirty tools. Likewise, boiling water, wiping with a towel or leaving tools in the sun does not sterilise them.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Read the **label** and the **safety data sheet (SDS)**: the maker's document on hazards, safe handling, storage and first aid.
Wear gloves, an apron and eye protection to mix and pour; open windows or use an extractor fan.
Keep chemicals in their own labelled containers; never put them into food or drink bottles.
**Never mix cleaning chemicals.** Bleach mixed with ammonia (found in some glass cleaners) or with acids gives off a poisonous gas.
Store chemicals in a cool, dry, ventilated place, away from heat, sunlight and food, and out of the reach of children.
If a chemical gets on the skin or in the eyes, rinse with plenty of clean water at once, and follow the SDS. Report it.

sections.title: Tools, equipment and the treatment area

head: Item
What to do after one client
rows: Metal tools that may break the skin (cuticle nippers, pushers, comedone extractors, tweezers)
Clean, then **sterilise** in an autoclave if the policy says; otherwise clean and disinfect for the full contact time. Store in a clean, closed container.
Metal tools that do not break skin (scissors, clippers)
Clean and disinfect
Porous or single-use items: emery boards, buffer blocks, wooden orange sticks, wax spatulas, cotton wool, couch roll, disposable gloves, eye pads, sponges
**Throw away** after one client, because they cannot be properly cleaned. A file may be given to the client to take home.
Plastic and glass items (brushes, bowls, applicators)
Clean and disinfect
Make-up brushes and applicators
Use clean disposable applicators; clean brushes between clients with a suitable brush cleaner and disinfect as the policy says
Foot bowl or foot spa
Drain, scrub, rinse, disinfect for the full contact time, rinse and dry. Flush pipes at the end of the day as the maker says.
Couch, chair and trolley
Cover with a fresh couch roll; wipe with detergent and disinfect between clients
Towels, gowns and headbands
Use clean ones for every client; used ones go into a closed laundry bin
Wax pot and wax
Never double dip a spatula; use a new spatula each time or a roll-on cartridge; clean and disinfect equipment as the maker says
Electrical equipment (steamers, high-frequency tips, machines)
Switch off and unplug; wipe or disinfect parts that touch skin as the maker says; never put the body of electrical equipment in water

ul: A tool that falls on the floor is **dirty**: clean and disinfect (or sterilise) it again before use.
Store clean tools in a clean, closed, labelled container, not in your pocket or loose on the trolley.
Keep **used** and **clean** tools apart: mark a tray 'used'.
Check tools before each use. Throw away or repair rusty, chipped or broken tools: they cannot be cleaned and can cause injury.

flow: Clean your hands and put on clean uniform and PPE
Clean and disinfect the couch, trolley, chair and any surface that will be touched
Put on a fresh couch roll and clean towels
Lay out clean, disinfected or sterile tools and fresh single-use items
Check the sharps box, bins and supplies
Ventilate the room; check the lighting
Place the waste bins and laundry bin within reach
Clean your hands; put on gloves and apron
Put used tools in the 'dirty' tray; put single-use items in the bin; used sharps in the sharps box
Put used towels in the closed laundry bin; remove the couch roll
Clean the surfaces with detergent; disinfect for the full contact time
Clean and disinfect or sterilise tools
Take off gloves; clean your hands
Prepare for the next client

ul: Empty and clean bins; remove waste and laundry; seal and store clinical waste.
Clean and disinfect all surfaces, sinks, taps, door handles, equipment, trolleys and floors.
Clean foot spas and flush them as the maker says; empty and clean wax pots as the maker says.
Change disinfectant solutions as the policy says; restock supplies.
Record the cleaning on the log.

blocks.p: Before every treatment, look at the skin, nails or area to be treated and ask about health, allergies and recent illness. This is the **consultation**. Some conditions are **contra-indications**: reasons why a treatment must not be given, or must be changed. A contagious condition stops the treatment.

head: Sign
Might be
What to do
rows: Honey-coloured crusts or weeping sores, around the nose, mouth or elsewhere
Impetigo (bacterial)
Do not treat; suggest she sees a doctor
Redness, swelling, heat, pus around a nail or hair follicle
Infection (bacterial, fungal)
Do not treat the area; refer her
Thick, yellow, crumbly, lifting nail
Fungal nail infection
Do not treat the nail; refer her to a doctor
Round, scaly, itchy patches
Ringworm (fungal)
Do not treat; refer her
Rough, raised growth on the hand or sole
Wart or verruca (viral)
Do not file, cut or treat the area; refer her
Blisters or tingling sores around the mouth
Cold sore (viral)
Do not treat the face; wait until healed
Very itchy rash, worse at night, between the fingers
Scabies (a mite)
Do not treat; refer her; take care of towels and tools
Itching, nits or lice in the hair
Head lice
Do not treat the scalp or face; refer her
Red, sticky, watery eyes
Conjunctivitis
Do not treat the eyes; refer her
Cuts, grazes, sunburn, recent surgery, bruising
Broken or damaged skin
Do not treat the area; wait until healed
Spreading redness, fever, swelling after a treatment
A possible new infection
Advise a doctor; record it

ul: You do not diagnose. Do not tell a client she has a named disease; describe what you see, and say that she should see a doctor or pharmacist.
Speak kindly and **in private**. Offer to rebook when she is better.
After a client with a contagious condition: bag towels for a hot wash, clean and disinfect all tools and surfaces that she touched, wash your hands, and write it down.
Do not use a tool on any area of the client's body if it has touched an infected area.

blocks.note: Do not use the same tool on an infected nail and on healthy nails, and never file or cut a wart. If a client's condition was not visible before and appears during the treatment, stop, explain kindly and apply the same rules.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Protecting clients with a high risk of infection

ul: A client with diabetes may heal slowly and have reduced feeling in her feet. Take special care with pedicures: no cutting or sharp tools, and advise her to see her doctor about any foot problem.
Be gentle with older clients and with those on medicines that thin the blood, because they bruise and bleed easily.
Check the client's own cuts before starting, and cover them if the treatment allows.

blocks.p: **Sharps** are items that can cut or pierce the skin: single-use blades, lancets, needles and the broken pieces of glass. The danger is a cut that puts blood from one person into another, because of hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.

ul: Use each blade on **one client only**, and put it straight into a **sharps box**: a rigid, puncture-proof, labelled container, kept upright near where sharps are used and out of reach of children.
Never recap, bend, break or pass a used blade by hand. Never leave one on the trolley or wrapped in a towel or tissue.
Never put a sharp into the ordinary bin, the paper recycling or a plastic bag.
Close the box when it reaches the **fill line** (about three-quarters full), not when it is overflowing, label it with the date and send it for collection by the approved service.
Never push the contents down with your hand. If a box is damaged or overfull, report it.

blocks.h: If you cut yourself or are splashed

flow: Let the wound bleed gently; do not suck or scrub it
Wash with soap and running water; cover with a waterproof dressing
For an eye splash, rinse with plenty of clean water; for a mouth splash, rinse and spit
Tell your supervisor at once
Seek medical advice quickly (the same day)
Complete the incident report and the sharps injury record

blocks.p: Treat every spill as if it is infectious. Use the salon's **spill kit**: gloves, apron, eye protection, absorbent granules or paper towels, a scoop, clinical waste bags, disinfectant and warning signs.

flow: Care for the client first; keep other people away from the spill
Put on gloves, apron and eye protection (and a mask if the policy says)
Cover the spill with absorbent granules or paper towels
Scoop up the soaked material into a clinical waste bag; do not use your hands
Clean the area with detergent and water
Disinfect it with the disinfectant that the policy names, for the full contact time
Put used PPE and cleaning material in the clinical waste bag; seal it
Wash your hands; replace the spill kit; record the spill

ul: For broken glass, wear gloves and sweep it up with a dustpan and brush. Never pick it up with bare hands. Put the glass in a rigid container.
Clean blood from a surface with disposable towels, not a cloth that you will reuse.
Never clean up blood with bare hands, and never wipe it with the towel that the client uses.

head: Type
Examples
Where it goes
rows: General waste
Paper, packaging, clean couch roll, empty product containers, food wrappers
A lined bin with a lid, emptied daily
Clinical (infectious) waste
Cotton wool, gloves, wax strips, tissues and dressings soiled with blood or body fluids
A clinical waste bag (as the Centre's policy colours it); seal when about three-quarters full; keep in a locked area; collected by the licensed service
Sharps
Used blades, lancets, needles, glass
A rigid sharps box
Chemical waste
Out-of-date or leftover products and disinfectant
As the product label and the policy say; never pour into drains where the label says not to
Recyclable waste
Clean cardboard, glass, plastic
As the Centre's recycling arrangements say

ul: Sort waste **where you make it**. Do not carry loose sharps or soiled items through the salon.
Do not overfill bags and boxes. Tie or seal bags when they are about three-quarters full.
Use bins with tight lids to keep out flies, rats and mosquitoes. Empty them daily.
Use a **clean towel and gown for every client**. Never reuse a used one, even if it looks clean.
Put used items into a **closed laundry bin** straight away. Do not shake them out, put them on the floor or back on a shelf. Handle with gloves if they are soiled.
Keep soiled (blood or body fluid) items in a separate, labelled bag.

Wash with detergent in **hot water**, as hot as the fabric allows (about 60 °C or above is a common guide), and dry completely, ideally in a hot dryer or in strong sun. Damp linen grows bacteria and mildew.
Store clean linen in a closed cupboard, away from dust, spray and dirty areas, off the floor.
Do not carry laundry across clean areas or leave it in a pile at the end of the day.
**Floors** should be smooth and washable; mop with detergent and disinfectant; do not sweep dry floors while clients are present.
**Surfaces and furniture** should be wipe-clean and in good repair: cracked or torn couch covers hold germs.
**Handwash basins** with hot and cold running water, liquid soap in a dispenser, paper towels and a bin should be near the treatment area. A bar of soap and a shared towel should not be used.
**Ventilation**: open windows, fans or an extractor fan, to move out chemical fumes and germs.
**Lighting**: good light helps you see dirt and skin conditions.
**Water**: use safe water. In a dry spell or when the supply is cut, you must still be able to wash hands and clean tools. If you cannot, do not carry out the treatment.
**Toilets**: clean daily, with soap and paper towels.
Flies, cockroaches and rats spread germs. Keep food and waste covered; wipe spills at once; seal holes and gaps; and follow the pest control plan.
Stop mosquitoes breeding by emptying or covering anything that holds water, including drums, tyres, plant saucers and gutters.
Do not keep food, drink or personal items in the treatment room.

blocks.note: Jamaica's heat and humidity make mildew and bacteria grow quickly on damp towels, sponges and brushes. Dry everything completely before storing it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Record
What it shows
rows: Cleaning schedule or log
That surfaces, equipment and rooms were cleaned and disinfected, when and by whom
Autoclave log
Date, cycle, temperature and time, and who ran it
Disinfectant log
When fresh solution was made, and the dilution
Client record card
Her details, contra-indications, patch tests, treatment given, products, and any reaction
Incident or accident report
Injuries, sharps injuries, blood spills, exposures, reactions and near misses
Waste records
Clinical waste and sharps collections
Training record
Who was trained in what, and when

ul: Fill in records **at the time**, clearly, in ink, and sign them. Do not write in advance. Never alter or hide a record; correct a mistake with one line, your initials and the date.
Records prove that procedures were followed, help trace a problem, and protect the salon and you if a complaint is made.
Keep client records private.
Any cut, sharps injury or splash of blood or body fluid, and any blood spill and how it was cleaned.
Signs of infection in a client or co-worker, and any client reaction or complaint of infection after a treatment.
Faulty equipment, such as an autoclave that is not working, a broken sink or a missing spill kit; short supplies of soap, gloves or paper towels.
A breach of the policy, or a near miss, such as a tool used without cleaning.

blocks.p: Report to your supervisor, in writing if the policy says so, as soon as possible. Do not blame or hide. Learning from errors keeps people safe.

head: The employer or Centre
You, the therapist or trainee
rows: Writes and updates the policy using Ministry of Health and Wellness guidance
Trains staff and keeps records
Provides handwash basins, soap, PPE, sharps boxes, spill kits, disinfectants and an autoclave
Maintains the premises; manages waste and pests
Reads, understands and follows the policy
Uses the equipment correctly
Asks when unsure, and reports problems
Attends training; keeps vaccinations up to date
Does not work when infectious

blocks.h: Showing clients that the salon is clean

ul: Clean your hands where the client can see you.
Take tools from a sealed pouch or a clean closed container, or open a new single-use item in front of her.
Explain, if she asks, how you clean your tools. Be honest and polite.
Never be offended if a client asks about hygiene. It is a good sign.
I can name the kinds of germ and give a salon example of a disease from each.
I can describe the chain of infection and say how good practice breaks it.
I can name the portals of entry, including broken skin.
I can explain standard precautions and why they apply to every client.
I can say where the IPC policy comes from, who must follow it and what to do if I think it is wrong.
I can clean my hands properly, and say when to use soap and water and when alcohol rub is enough.
I can choose, put on and take off PPE correctly, and change gloves between clients.
I can explain the difference between cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation, with an example of each.
I can clean, disinfect and store metal tools correctly, including contact time and dilution.
I can say what an autoclave does and what a UV cabinet does not do.
I can say which items are single-use and why.
I can prepare a treatment area, reset it between clients and clean it at the end of the day.
I can handle chemicals safely and know why never to mix them.
I can recognise signs of infection in a client and refer her kindly.
I can use a sharps box and say when it must be closed.
I can deal with a blood spill with a spill kit, and with broken glass.
I can say what to do if I cut myself on a used blade.
I can sort general, clinical, sharps and chemical waste.
I can handle towels and laundry safely.
I can complete cleaning records and incident reports, and say what must be reported.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. Example: 'I scrub the tweezers before I disinfect them, because dirt and product stop the disinfectant reaching the germs.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The habits and procedures that stop germs spreading.
The salon's written rules; the procedures say how to follow them.
A germ that can cause disease.
A living thing too small to see without a microscope, such as bacteria and viruses.
A tough form made by some bacteria that only sterilisation can be relied on to kill.
The links by which a germ passes from one person to another.
A way into the body, such as a cut, the eyes, nose or mouth.
Spread by touching an infected person.
Spread through an object, such as a towel or a tool.
Safe steps used with every client, every time.
Gloves, aprons, masks and eye protection.
Removing dirt, hair and product with detergent and water.
Killing most germs on clean tools and surfaces with a chemical.
How long an item must stay wet with disinfectant for it to work.
A machine that sterilises tools with steam under pressure.
A cabinet used to store tools that are already clean and disinfected.
Used on one client only, then thrown away.
Putting a used wax spatula back into the wax pot.
The maker's document on a chemical's hazards, safe use, storage and first aid.
A reason why a treatment must not be given, or must be changed.
Items that can cut or pierce the skin, such as blades and needles.
A rigid, puncture-proof, labelled container for used sharps.
Equipment for cleaning up blood and body fluid safely.
Waste soiled with blood or body fluids.
A virus carried in blood, such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.
A written record of an injury, spill, exposure or near miss.
An event that could have caused harm but did not.

c1.title: Resetting a nail bar in Half Way Tree
c1.text: At a busy nail bar in Half Way Tree, Kingston, trainee Renee has just finished a manicure and pedicure. The next client, Mrs Lorna Gordon, is waiting. Renee wants to rinse her cuticle nippers under the tap, wipe them on a towel and put them in the UV cabinet. A foot bowl still has water in it, and there are used emery boards and orange sticks on the trolley.

c2.title: A nick during a brow clean-up in Portmore
c2.text: At a salon in Portmore, therapist Tamara uses a single-use blade to tidy a client's brow and nicks the client's skin, which bleeds a little. A drop of blood falls on the floor, and another spot lands on the headband. Tamara wipes the floor with a damp cloth, puts the blade, wrapped in tissue, into the ordinary bin and carries on. The sharps box is on the shelf, and the spill kit is in the cupboard.

c3.title: The chemicals shelf in Mandeville
c3.text: In a salon in Mandeville, junior therapist Deion needs more disinfectant for soaking tools, so he mixes the last of the old bleach cleaner with a glass cleaner to make it 'stronger', and pours it into an old drinks bottle. The disinfectant label gives a dilution of 1 part to 20 parts water and a contact time of 10 minutes. The bleach is stored on a sunny windowsill. The salon's safety data sheets are in a drawer in the manager's office.

c4.title: A client with a foot problem in Spanish Town
c4.text: Mrs Pearl Dixon, 64, has booked a pedicure at a salon in Spanish Town. She has diabetes. Her big toenail is thick, yellow and crumbly, and there is a rough, raised growth on the sole of her foot. Therapist Anika thinks that she can file the growth down and treat the toenail 'to make her feel better'.

c5.title: Closing time at a spa in Negril
c5.text: At a spa in Negril, the last client has left. Therapist Shaun puts used towels back on the shelf to use again, drops wax strips stained with blood into the general bin, and leaves the foot spa water in the bowl overnight. The sharps box is nearly full to the top, with a blade sticking out. The bins have no lids.

c6.title: Inspection day in Kingston
c6.text: A health inspector is due at the Centre's training salon. The supervisor, Miss Francine Rhoden, asks the trainees to be ready. A new trainee, Joel, says that he saw a video that says to rinse tools in hot water, and he asks whether the Centre's policy is really necessary. The cleaning log has gaps for two days, and Ricardo says he will fill them in now from memory.

questions.q: What is the correct order for Renee to deal with the cuticle nippers?
o: Scrub in soapy water, rinse and dry, then disinfect or sterilise
Rinse under the tap, wipe dry, then keep them in the UV cabinet to be clean
Disinfect for the contact time, then scrub, rinse and store them dry
Wipe with a damp towel, then leave them in disinfectant until the next client
questions.why: Always clean before you disinfect or sterilise, because dirt and product protect germs and use up the disinfectant. A UV cabinet only stores tools that are already clean and disinfected.

questions.q: What should Renee do about the foot bowl?
o: Top up the water and add a little fresh soap for Mrs Gordon's feet
Rinse it once with the hose and leave it to dry in the sun
Wipe the rim with a damp towel and then refill it with fresh water
Drain it, scrub it, disinfect it for the contact time, rinse and dry
questions.why: Water left in a foot bowl can carry germs from the last client. The bowl must be drained, scrubbed, disinfected for the contact time and dried before the next client.

questions.q: Renee still has her used gloves on. What must she do before she starts on Mrs Gordon?
o: Wipe the gloves with alcohol rub and keep them on for Mrs Gordon
Keep the gloves on, as they will protect Mrs Gordon as well
Remove the used gloves, clean her hands and put on new ones
Put a second pair of gloves over the first pair to be safe
questions.why: Gloves are changed between clients because germs stay on them. Clean your hands after taking them off and before putting on a new pair; gloves are never reused or wiped.

questions.q: Mrs Gordon asks, 'How do I know your tools are clean?' What is the best answer from Renee?
o: 'Please don't worry, we have never had a problem in this salon.'
'They come from a sealed pouch, and I can show you how we clean them.'
'That is a trade secret, and only the manager can discuss it.'
'I only ever use tools that look clean to me, so you can relax.'
questions.why: A client who asks about hygiene should get a polite and honest answer. Showing a sealed pouch or a clean closed container, and explaining the steps, builds trust.

questions.q: Tamara has wiped the blood drop off the floor with a damp cloth. What should she have done?
o: Use the spill kit: gloves, cover, scoop, clean, then disinfect
Spray perfume on the spot and mop the whole floor at the end of the day
Wipe it with the same damp cloth that she used to clean the couch
Walk round the spot until the cleaner comes in at night to deal with it
questions.why: Blood is treated as infectious. Use the spill kit, scoop the soaked material into clinical waste, clean with detergent and then disinfect for the contact time. A reusable cloth spreads germs.

questions.q: Why is it wrong to wrap the used blade in tissue and put it in the ordinary bin?
o: Tissue is not strong enough to hold a blade safely in the bin
The bin will fill up faster if blades are put in with the rubbish
The blade will blunt the other items in the bin and spoil them
Someone handling the bin could be cut, and a virus could pass on
questions.why: A used blade is a sharp that may carry blood. It must go straight into a rigid, puncture-proof sharps box, never into a bag or the general bin where cleaners and waste collectors could be cut.

questions.q: What should happen to the headband that has a spot of blood on it?
o: Fold it up and put it away with the clean headbands on the shelf
Rinse it in cold water and hang it outside to dry in the sun
Bag it separately and wash it hot, apart from other linen
Put it in the general bin as it is cheaper to replace than to wash
questions.why: Blood-soiled linen is kept apart and washed hot with detergent so the germs are killed. Cold rinsing and reusing it, or mixing it with clean items, spreads germs.

questions.q: What is the main danger of mixing the bleach cleaner with the glass cleaner?
o: It makes the mixture weaker, so it no longer disinfects well
A poisonous gas can form that harms the lungs and eyes
It will leave a sticky film on the tools that is hard to rinse off
It will stain the sink and the floor where it is poured
questions.why: Bleach mixed with ammonia, found in many glass cleaners, or with acids, gives off a poisonous gas. Never mix cleaning chemicals; use each one as the label says.

questions.q: The label says 1 part disinfectant to 20 parts water. Deion wants to use 50 mL of disinfectant. How much water does he need?
o: 500 mL
100 mL
questions.why: For every 1 part of disinfectant you add 20 parts of water. 50 mL x 20 = 1000 mL, so 1 litre of water. Too weak a solution does not kill the germs.

questions.q: The contact time is 10 minutes. Deion puts the first tool in the solution at 2:10 p.m. and the last one in at 2:15 p.m. When can he take them all out?
o: At 2:20 p.m., because 10 minutes have passed since the first tool
At 2:15 p.m., because all the tools are in
At 2:25 p.m., 10 minutes after the last tool went in
At 2:30 p.m., because it is safer to double the time
questions.why: The contact time runs from when the last tool is completely covered, so that every tool has the full time. Leaving some tools in for too long can also damage them.

questions.q: What is wrong with keeping the safety data sheets in a drawer in the manager's office?
o: Nothing is wrong, because only the manager handles the chemicals here
They should be kept in the stock room with the bleach and cleaners
Staff need quick access in a spill or splash, so copies must be easy to reach
They should be locked away so that clients cannot read about the products
questions.why: The safety data sheet gives first aid and clean-up information, which is needed at once if a chemical spills or splashes. Keep a copy where all staff can find it.

questions.q: Mrs Dixon's toenail is thick, yellow and crumbly. What should Anika do?
o: File the nail thin, then disinfect the file and throw it away
Not treat the nail; explain kindly in private and refer her
Paint the nail with a thick polish to cover the colour
Give the pedicure but work around the bad toe with clean tools
questions.why: These are signs of a possible fungal infection, which is a contra-indication. Working on it could spread it to other nails and to other clients through tools. Refer her without naming the disease.

questions.q: Why does Mrs Dixon's diabetes call for extra care with a pedicure?
o: She heals slowly and may not feel a cut, so it can become infected
Diabetes makes the nails grow very fast, so she needs more visits
Diabetes makes disinfectants less effective on her skin and nails
Clients with diabetes are only allowed shorter treatments by law
questions.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling in the feet and slow healing, so even a tiny cut can become a serious infection. Avoid cutting or sharp tools and advise her to see her doctor about foot problems.

questions.q: How should Anika tell Mrs Dixon that she cannot give the treatment today?
o: Loudly at the desk so that the other clients take care too
By telling her it is a fungus and that she must stop coming here
By saying the salon is too busy today and giving no other reason
Quietly, in private, describing what she sees and suggesting a doctor
questions.why: A therapist does not diagnose. Speak kindly in private, explain that the treatment could make the problem worse or spread it, suggest a doctor and offer to rebook. Record it on her card.

questions.q: What should Shaun do with the used towels?
o: Shake them out and hang them up to air ready for tomorrow
Put them back on the shelf if they look clean enough
Put them in a closed laundry bin for a hot wash
Leave them on the couch until the weekend wash day
questions.why: Towels carry germs from the skin, even when they look clean. Put them straight into a closed laundry bin and wash them hot with detergent.

questions.q: The sharps box is almost full, and a blade is sticking out of the top. What should be done?
o: Push the blade down with a gloved hand to make a little more room
Close and label it at the fill line, and start a new box
Tape a second box on top of it so that it can be used again
Cover the top with a carrier bag and carry on using the box
questions.why: A sharps box is closed at the fill line, never overfilled. Never push the contents down, because that can cut you. Label the box with the date and send it for collection.

questions.q: Why is it wrong to leave the foot spa water in the bowl overnight?
o: Standing water grows germs that the next client will meet
The bowl will crack in the cool night air and have to be replaced
It will use too much electricity if the pump is left running
It will leave marks on the plastic that are hard to clean off
questions.why: Warm, dirty water is where bacteria multiply quickly. Drain, scrub, disinfect and dry the bowl, and flush the pipes as the maker says, at the end of each day.

questions.q: Joel says he saw a video that says rinsing tools in hot water is enough. How should Miss Rhoden answer?
o: The video is fine, as the policy is just a guide that can be changed
Hot water is enough for plastic, but metal tools need disinfectant
The policy is for the inspector only, and does not apply to daily work
Hot water alone does not kill all germs; the policy follows health guidance
questions.why: Rinsing is not cleaning, and hot tap water does not disinfect or sterilise. The Centre's policy is based on Ministry of Health and Wellness guidance and the makers' instructions, so follow it, not an unverified video.

questions.q: Ricardo says he will fill the two gap days in the cleaning log from memory. What should he do instead?
o: Fill them in as if done on the day, so the log looks complete
Tear out the page and start a new one before the inspector comes
Leave the gaps, tell Miss Rhoden, and record today's date honestly
Ask another trainee to write them in as she remembers them
questions.why: Records must be true and made at the time. A false entry is dishonest and defeats the purpose of the log. Report the gap, put it right and record the real date.

questions.q: A therapist says, 'She looks healthy, so I don't need gloves for this wax.' Which principle does this break?
o: The rule that single-use items are used for one client only
The same safe steps for every client (standard precautions)
The rule that tools are cleaned before they are disinfected
The rule that the client's skin is checked before treatment
questions.why: You cannot tell by looking whether a person carries hepatitis B or HIV. Standard precautions mean using the same safe steps for every client, whether she looks well or not.
